Gaussian processes are rich distributions over
functions, which provide a Bayesian nonpara-
metric approach to smoothing and interpola-
tion. We introduce simple closed form ker-
nels that can be used with Gaussian pro-
cesses to discover patterns and enable extrap-
olation. These kernels are derived by mod-
elling a spectral density – the Fourier trans-
form of a kernel – with a Gaussian mixture.
The proposed kernels support a broad class
of stationary covariances, but Gaussian pro-
cess inference remains simple and analytic.
We demonstrate the proposed kernels by dis-
covering patterns and performing long range
extrapolation on synthetic examples, as well
as atmospheric CO2 trends and airline pas-
senger data. We also show that it is possible
to reconstruct several popular standard co-
variances within our framework.

## Answer: Gaussian process kernels

The corpus contains one paper directly and substantively about this topic — **Wilson & Adams, *"Gaussian Process Kernels for Pattern Discovery and Extrapolation"*** (`1302.4245.pdf`). Every other corpus hit uses "kernel" in an unrelated sense (CNN convolution kernels, memory/convolution kernels in physics, or "Gaussian kernel methods" mentioned in passing), so the answer below is drawn from that one paper, cited by page.

### The problem with standard GP kernels
A Gaussian process is a Bayesian nonparametric distribution over functions; the properties of those functions — smoothness, periodicity, etc. — are set entirely by the **covariance (kernel) function** (p. 3). The most popular choice, the **squared exponential (SE)** kernel, `k_SE(x,x') = exp(−0.5‖x−x'‖²/ℓ²)`, produces infinitely-differentiable functions and acts merely as a *smoothing device*: the only structure learnable from data is the length-scale ℓ (p. 3). In the standard workflow a human looks at the data, recognizes patterns, and hand-codes them into the kernel — the GP itself does no pattern discovery (p. 4, CO₂ discussion).

### The core idea — the Spectral Mixture (SM) kernel
The paper's contribution is a closed-form family of stationary kernels that let the GP *discover* patterns and extrapolate, while keeping inference simple and analytic (Abstract, p. 1).

The derivation (p. 3):
- **Bochner's theorem** says any stationary kernel is the Fourier dual of a spectral density S(s): `k(τ) = ∫ S(s) e^{2πis·τ} ds` (Eqs. 6–8).
- An SE kernel corresponds only to a Gaussian spectral density centered at the origin — "a very small corner of the set of possible stationary kernels."
- Since **mixtures of Gaussians are dense in the set of all distributions**, modelling the spectral density as a *scale-location mixture of Gaussians* (with non-zero means) can approximate any stationary kernel to arbitrary precision.

Taking the Fourier transform back gives the closed-form **spectral mixture kernel** (Eqs. 11–12, pp. 3–4):

  k(τ) = Σ_{q=1}^Q w_q ∏_{p=1}^P exp{−2π²τ_p² v_q^{(p)}} · cos(2π τ_p μ_q^{(p)})

The hyperparameters are directly interpretable (p. 4): weights **w_q** = each component's relative contribution; inverse means **1/μ_q** = component periods; inverse standard deviations **1/√v_q** = length-scales. It is a "drop-in replacement" for the kernels in Rasmussen & Williams (2006). Training uses conjugate-gradient optimization of the marginal likelihood, and **automatic relevance determination** prunes unneeded components (p. 4).

### Evidence it works (experiments, pp. 4–7)
- **Atmospheric CO₂ (Mauna Loa):** With Q=10 (only 7 components retained), the SM kernel discovers the yearly period (peak near 12 months) plus 6-/4-/3-/1-month structure and extrapolates ≈25 years ahead; the 95% predictive region contains the true test data, while SE/Matérn/RQ/periodic kernels only interpolate (pp. 4–5).
- **Recovering popular kernels:** With Q≤10 the SM kernel closely reconstructs standard kernels — e.g. a Matérn (ν=3/2) correlation function (Eq. 13) and a sum of RQ + periodic kernels (p. 5, Fig. 2).
- **Negative covariances:** It recovers the covariance of an oscillatory AR(1) process, identifying a spectral peak at frequency 0.5 (period 2) (p. 7, Eqs. 16–18).
- **Sinc pattern:** From 700 training points it reconstructs a three-sinc pattern almost perfectly over a gap the competing kernels entirely miss (p. 7, Eq. 19).

### One-line summary
The corpus's answer to "Gaussian process kernels" is Wilson & Adams' **spectral mixture kernel**: by modelling a GP's spectral density as a Gaussian mixture, you get a simple closed-form, interpretable stationary kernel that can represent essentially any stationary covariance and thereby lets a GP discover patterns and extrapolate rather than just smooth (`1302.4245.pdf`, Abstract p. 1; derivation pp. 3–4; experiments pp. 4–7).
